title: Sleepy Stories for Grown-Ups 🌙 Rain, Tea and Quiet Places | Snortlo
intro: Hello, and welcome. This is Snortlo, and tonight I have six quiet stories for you, about rain, and tea, and gentle places. Before we start, let yourself get comfortable. Turn the lights down low, or switch them off. Let your head sink a little deeper into the pillow. There is nothing left to do today. It is all done, or it can wait until tomorrow. You don't need to listen to every word, and you don't need to stay awake until the end. If you drift off along the way, that is perfect. Take one slow breath in. And let it all the way out. Let's begin.

stories.title: The Late Bus
stories.text:
The last bus of the night left the depot at a quarter past eleven. It was the number nine, though nobody in town ever called it that. They called it the late bus, or the slow bus, or, if they were feeling fond of it, the old girl. Walt had been driving it for nearly twenty years.

He liked the late route best. In the daytime the bus was busy and loud, full of shopping bags and school bags and people talking on their phones. But at night the town grew quiet, and the bus grew quiet with it, and the whole route seemed to soften, like a sweater that has been washed many times.

Tonight there was a fine mist in the air. It was not quite rain. It was the kind of weather that settles on your coat in tiny silver beads and makes the streetlights look as if they are wearing halos. Walt turned on the wipers, and they went back and forth, slow and steady, swish and pause, swish and pause.

He pulled out of the depot and onto Mill Road. The shops were all closed. The bakery had its blinds down. The hardware store had one small lamp on in the back, the way it always did, as if someone had forgotten it years ago and nobody had the heart to turn it off.

The first stop was outside the library. Nobody was waiting there, but Walt slowed down anyway and opened the doors for a moment, because that was what he always did. The cool air came in, smelling of wet leaves. He counted to three, closed the doors, and drove on.

At the second stop, by the little park with the fountain, the first of his regulars was waiting. She was an older woman in a long green coat, and she carried a cloth bag with knitting needles poking out of the top. Walt did not know her name. She did not know his. In all the years she had been riding the late bus, they had never had a conversation. But every night she climbed the steps, tapped her card, and gave him a small, warm nod, and every night he nodded back.

She sat in her usual seat, the third one on the left, by the window. Before the bus had even pulled away, the knitting needles were out, and the soft clicking began. Click, click, click. It was a very peaceful sound. Walt sometimes thought the bus ran a little smoother when she was knitting.

They drove along the river. The water was dark and still, and the lights from the bridge lay on top of it in long, wobbly lines. A heron was standing in the shallows near the bank, perfectly still, with its neck tucked in. Walt had seen it there many times. He liked to think it was waiting for a bus of its own.

At the corner of Hill Street, the second regular got on. He was a young man in a hospital uniform, pale blue, with a soft jacket over the top. He always looked tired, but it was the good kind of tired, the kind that comes from a long day of being useful. He tapped his card, gave Walt a little wave with two fingers, and went all the way to the back, where he stretched out his legs and leaned his head against the window.

Within a few minutes his eyes were closed. Walt never woke him. He knew exactly where the young man got off, at the top of Orchard Lane, and when they got close he would take the last corner a little more slowly and let the brakes sigh a little louder, and the young man would open his eyes, stretch, and stand up, just in time. It had worked every night for three years.

The bus climbed the long hill past the school. The windows of the school were dark, and the playground was empty, and the swings moved just a little in the breeze, as if they were remembering the afternoon. At the top of the hill, the whole town spread out below, a scattering of warm yellow windows and orange streetlights, with the river curling through it like a ribbon.

Walt always took a breath at the top of the hill. He did not stop the bus, but he let it roll a little slower, and he looked out at the town, and he thought, there you all are. Everyone tucked in. Everyone home.

The third regular got on at the stop by the bakery on Orchard Lane, the other bakery, the one that opened very early. She was a baker herself, a cheerful woman with flour on her sleeves, even at this hour, and she always carried a paper bag. She tapped her card, nodded, and sat in the front seat, the one just behind Walt.

She never said anything. But at the end of her ride, every single night, she would leave the paper bag on the little ledge beside the driver's seat. Inside there would be something warm. A bread roll. A cinnamon knot. Once, on a very cold night, a small apple pie with a crust shaped like a leaf.

Walt had tried to thank her many times. He had tried to wave, to call out, to leave a note. But she was always off the bus and walking away into the dark before he could manage it, and she never looked back. So in the end he had decided that the best way to thank her was to drive her home as gently as he possibly could.

The bus went on through the quiet streets. The knitting needles clicked. The young man in the back slept with his mouth a little open. The baker looked out the window and hummed something under her breath, so quietly that Walt could only just hear it. The wipers swished and paused. The engine made its low, contented rumble.

Near the top of Orchard Lane, Walt slowed the bus, and let the brakes sigh, and the young man woke up, stretched, and walked down the aisle. At the doors, he turned and gave the two finger wave again, and Walt waved back. The doors folded open. The young man stepped out into the mist and walked off toward a row of little houses, where one porch light was already on, waiting for him.

The knitter got off at the next stop. She put her needles away, tucked her bag under her arm, and gave Walt her usual nod. He nodded back. As she walked away, he noticed that the knitting in her bag was a long scarf in a deep, soft blue, almost the color of his driver's jacket. He wondered, for a moment, who it was for. Then the doors closed, and he drove on.

The baker was last, as always. At the corner by the bakery, she stood, smoothed her coat, and placed the paper bag on the ledge. Walt opened his mouth to say thank you, but she was already down the steps and into the mist, a small shape walking toward the warm glow of the bakery windows.

Walt drove the empty bus back down the hill, along the river, past the heron, who had not moved at all, and into the depot. He parked the bus in its usual spot, turned off the engine, and sat for a moment in the quiet.

Then he opened the paper bag. Inside, wrapped in a napkin, was a small, round loaf of bread, still warm. And folded beside it was something soft. He lifted it out. It was the blue scarf. There was a little tag pinned to one end, with neat handwriting on it. For the driver of the late bus, it said. From the three of us.

Walt sat in the dark bus for a long time with the scarf in his hands. Then he wrapped it around his neck, and it was warm, and it smelled faintly of bread and wool. He switched off the last light, and the old girl settled into her parking spot with a soft creak, and the depot was quiet, and outside the mist went on falling, gently, over the sleeping town.

stories.title: The Beekeeper's Blankets
stories.text:
At the far end of a long meadow, where the grass ran down to a line of old apple trees, there were seven beehives. They were painted in different colors, because Mabel had painted them herself over the years, whenever she had a little leftover paint. There was a yellow one, a pale green one, a sky blue one, a pink one that had faded almost to white, a red one, a cream one, and one that was painted half blue and half green, because she had run out of blue partway through.

Mabel was not young anymore, but she was not old either, or at least she did not feel old. She felt like someone who had been doing the same gentle thing for a long time and had gotten good at it. She had kept bees for thirty years. She knew the sound of a happy hive, a low, warm hum, like a kettle just before it starts to sing. And she knew the sound of a hive that was settling down for the winter, which was quieter, and slower, and somehow more patient.

It was the last afternoon of autumn, or it felt like it. The air had a sharp, clean coldness in it, and the sky was very pale, almost silver. The apple trees had dropped most of their leaves, and the leaves lay in soft brown piles around the trunks. A few late apples still hung on the high branches, small and red, like ornaments someone had forgotten to take down.

Mabel walked down the meadow with a wheelbarrow. In the wheelbarrow there were blankets. They were old blankets, the kind you find at the bottom of a cupboard. A grey one with a hole in the corner. A checked one in red and brown. A very soft yellow one that had once belonged to her mother. A patchwork quilt that had seen better days. She had washed them all and dried them in the sun, and now they were folded in a neat pile, and they smelled of fresh air.

Her dog, a slow and serious old sheepdog named Henry, walked beside the wheelbarrow. Henry did not like the bees very much, and the bees did not think much of Henry, but at this time of year the bees mostly stayed indoors, and so Henry was willing to come along and supervise.

At the first hive, the yellow one, Mabel stopped and put her ear close to the wood. She did not need to open it. She could hear the hum inside, low and steady. The bees were clustered together in the middle of the hive, she knew, in a warm ball, with the queen safe in the center. They would stay like that all winter, gently shivering to make heat, taking turns on the cold outside of the cluster and then moving into the warm middle again. Mabel had always thought that was one of the kindest things she knew of. Nobody had to stay cold for long. Everybody took a turn.

She tapped the side of the hive twice, very softly, the way she always did. Then she took the grey blanket from the wheelbarrow, shook it out, and wrapped it around the hive, leaving the little doorway at the bottom clear, so the bees could come and go on a warm day. She tied the blanket in place with a length of garden string, and tucked in the corners neatly, like a bed.

Henry watched all of this very seriously. When she had finished, he sniffed the corner of the blanket, sneezed, and sat down. That meant he approved.

They went on to the next hive, the pale green one, and the next, the sky blue one. At each hive Mabel listened, and tapped twice, and wrapped a blanket around it, and tied it with string. The checked blanket went on the green hive. The patchwork quilt went on the blue one. She talked to the bees while she worked, quietly, the way you might talk to someone who is half asleep. She told them that it had been a good year. That the clover had been lovely in June. That the honey was in jars on the kitchen shelf, catching the light, and that she would think of them every time she spread some on her toast.

There is an old idea that you should tell the bees your news. Mabel did not know if the bees understood, but she told them anyway. She told them that her niece had written to say she was coming to visit at the new year. That the roof of the shed had finally been fixed. That Henry had been very good this autumn, mostly. Henry, hearing his name, thumped his tail on the ground.

By the time they reached the pink hive, the sun was getting low. It hung just above the line of the far hills, a soft orange circle, and the light came across the meadow sideways, making every blade of grass glow. Mabel's shadow stretched out very long beside her, and Henry's shadow stretched out beside his, and for a moment they looked like two tall strangers walking together through a golden field.

The pink hive got the yellow blanket, the soft one that had been her mother's. Mabel held it for a moment before she wrapped it, and she smiled, because her mother had kept bees too, and had taught her everything she knew, and would have liked to see the blanket being used this way. Then she wrapped the hive, and tied it, and tapped twice, and moved on.

The red hive and the cream hive got the last two blankets, a brown one and a faded blue one. Then there was only the half blue and half green hive left, and Mabel looked into the wheelbarrow and realized that she had run out of blankets.

She stood for a moment, thinking. Henry looked up at her. The sun slid a little lower behind the hills.

Then Mabel unwound the long woolen scarf from around her own neck. It was a thick, warm scarf, striped in blue and green, which, now that she looked at it, was almost exactly the color of the hive. She laughed quietly to herself. She wrapped the scarf around the hive, around and around, and tied the ends in a neat bow at the front, just above the little doorway.

It looked a little silly. It looked like a hive that was getting ready to go skating. But it looked warm, and that was the important thing.

She tapped twice on the wood. From inside, the hum went on, low and patient and steady.

Mabel put the empty wheelbarrow back in the shed. She and Henry walked up the meadow together as the sky turned from orange to pink to a deep, soft blue. The first star came out above the apple trees. Behind them, the seven hives sat in a row in the dusk, each one bundled up in its blanket, like a row of little houses with their lights turned down.

In the kitchen, Mabel lit the stove and put the kettle on. She made a cup of tea with a spoonful of honey in it, and sat by the window with Henry at her feet. Outside, the meadow was dark now, and quiet. Somewhere out there, in seven warm hives, thousands of bees were gently taking turns, moving from the cold edge to the warm middle and back again, all through the long night.

Mabel drank her tea slowly. Henry sighed and stretched out on the rug. The kettle ticked as it cooled. And down at the end of the meadow, under the bare apple trees and the slowly turning stars, the hives hummed softly, all winter long.

stories.title: The Snowed In Inn
stories.text:
The snow started just after lunch, and by four o'clock in the afternoon, the road down the valley had disappeared completely. It did not happen all at once. First the fields turned white, then the stone walls, then the fence posts got little white caps, and then, quietly, the road itself simply faded away, as if someone had gently rubbed it out with an eraser.

The inn sat halfway up the valley, a long, low stone building with a slate roof and a crooked chimney. It was called the Hollow Inn, and it had been there for longer than anyone could remember. Mrs. Lowe ran it now. She was a small, brisk, kind woman who wore an apron at all times and seemed to know exactly what everyone needed before they knew it themselves.

That evening there were five guests at the inn, and none of them were going anywhere.

There was a retired schoolteacher named Mr. Pell, who had come to walk in the hills and was now very happy not to. There was a young couple on their way to visit family, who had stopped for a cup of tea and stayed for the snow. There was a quiet woman named June, who was writing a book and said very little about it. And there was a man named Theo, who sold garden furniture and had been driving through the valley when the snow got too thick, and who had arrived at the door with snow up to his knees and an expression of polite astonishment.

Mrs. Lowe gathered them all in the big front room. There was a fireplace at one end, wide enough to stand in, and the fire was already roaring. The room smelled of wood smoke and old books and something wonderful drifting in from the kitchen. The windows were small and deep set, and outside them the snow fell steadily, big soft flakes drifting down past the glass, lit gold by the lamps inside.

The roads will be closed until morning, Mrs. Lowe told them. Possibly the afternoon. So you are all my guests tonight, and there is soup.

There was, indeed, soup. It came out in a great iron pot, and Mrs. Lowe ladled it into deep blue bowls. It was a thick vegetable soup with barley and herbs, and there was fresh bread to go with it, with a crust that crackled when you broke it, and butter in a little dish. Everyone sat around the long wooden table by the fire and ate slowly, and nobody said very much at first, because the soup was too good to interrupt.

After the soup there was apple crumble with cream. After the crumble there was tea, in a big brown teapot with a knitted cover. And after the tea, Mrs. Lowe went to a cupboard in the corner and came back with a large, flat box.

It was a jigsaw puzzle. One thousand pieces, the box said. On the lid there was a picture of a harbor at sunset, with little boats and a long stone pier and a sky full of pink and orange clouds.

It has been in that cupboard for six years, Mrs. Lowe said. Nobody has ever finished it. I am not sure all the pieces are there. But we have all night.

They cleared the table and tipped the pieces out. They made a soft, rattling, whispering sound as they spread across the wood, a sound like light rain on a roof. Mr. Pell immediately began turning all the pieces face up, very methodically, one at a time. The young couple started looking for edges. June sorted the sky pieces into a little pile of pinks and a little pile of oranges. Theo picked up a single piece, looked at it from every side, and announced that it was definitely part of a boat. It was not. It was part of a cloud. Everyone laughed, and Theo laughed the most.

Outside, the snow kept falling. The wind had dropped completely, and the flakes came straight down, slow and heavy, piling up on the windowsills in soft white cushions.

The edges came together first, as edges do. Then the pier, which was mostly grey and brown and surprisingly difficult. Then the boats, one by one. Mr. Pell did the red boat. The young couple did the blue one together, their heads bent close. June, without a word, finished most of the sky, and every now and then she would hold up a piece, look at it against the lamplight, and slot it into place with a tiny, satisfied click.

Mrs. Lowe came and went. She put more wood on the fire. She brought out a plate of shortbread. She lit two more lamps. At one point she brought Theo a pair of thick wool socks, because his own were still damp from the snow, and he put them on and wiggled his toes by the fire and said they were the best socks he had ever worn.

The clock on the mantelpiece ticked. The fire popped and settled. The puzzle grew slowly, from the edges in, like a picture coming up through still water.

At some point, late in the evening, the young woman from the couple fell asleep in her chair, with her head on her husband's shoulder. He did not move, so as not to wake her, and went on doing the puzzle with one hand. Mr. Pell yawned enormously and apologized. June took off her glasses, rubbed her eyes, put them back on, and kept going.

By eleven o'clock, there was only a small patch of water left in the middle of the harbor, and a scattering of pieces on the table. They fitted them in one at a time, slowly, passing pieces back and forth. The water was all the same dark blue, and every piece looked exactly like every other piece, and it took a long time.

Finally there was one gap left. One empty space, right in the middle of the harbor, under the red boat.

And there were no pieces left on the table.

They looked under the table. They looked under the chairs. They looked in the box, and under the box, and in the folds of the tablecloth. Theo checked his pockets, just in case. Nothing.

I knew it, said Mrs. Lowe. Six years. One piece missing. I always thought so.

They all sat back and looked at the puzzle. It was very beautiful, even with the hole. The little boats, the long pier, the glowing sky.

Then Theo, who had been looking at the floor near the fire, bent down and picked something up. It had been tucked inside one of the wool socks Mrs. Lowe had given him, and it had fallen out when he stretched his feet toward the warmth. He held it up to the lamp. It was a small piece of dark blue water.

Nobody said anything. Theo leaned forward and put the piece into the gap, and pressed it down gently with one finger, and it fit perfectly, with a tiny, soft click.

The puzzle was finished. For the first time in six years, the harbor was whole.

Mrs. Lowe looked at it for a long moment, and then she smiled, and said, well, I think that calls for cocoa. And she went to make some.

They drank the cocoa by the fire, and admired the puzzle, and nobody wanted to be the first to go to bed. But the fire burned down to a warm orange glow, and the lamps seemed to dim a little on their own, and one by one, the guests drifted upstairs to their rooms, with their heavy quilts and their little windows full of falling snow.

Mrs. Lowe was the last one up. She did not put the puzzle away. She left it on the table, finished, beside the sleeping fire. Then she turned off the last lamp, and the room went soft and dark, and outside, the snow went on falling over the valley, quietly covering the roads, and the walls, and the fields, and the whole sleeping inn, like a blanket being pulled gently up to the chin.

stories.title: The Last Ferry
stories.text:
The lake was so still that evening that it looked like a second sky. The real sky was turning the color of peaches, and the lake turned the color of peaches with it, and the line between them, far away at the other end, was so faint that you could hardly tell where one stopped and the other began.

The ferry crossed the lake four times a day. It was not a big ferry. It was a wide, flat, wooden boat with a little roof at one end and benches along the sides, and a small engine that went putt, putt, putt, never in any hurry. It could carry about twenty people, or a few bicycles, or on one memorable occasion a piano, very carefully. The ferryman was called Arthur, and he had been crossing the lake for most of his life.

The last crossing of the day was at dusk. It was usually the quietest one. Tonight there were only three passengers. A woman with a basket of eggs from one of the farms on the far shore. A boy of about ten, going home to his grandmother's house after a day of fishing, with a rod over his shoulder and absolutely no fish. And a man in a tidy coat who had clearly never been on the ferry before, because he was holding onto the rail as if the lake might suddenly decide to do something surprising.

Arthur untied the rope from the dock, coiled it neatly, and pushed off. The engine went putt, putt, putt. The ferry slid out onto the glassy water, and behind it a long, soft V spread out across the lake, rippling the peach colored sky into gentle folds.

They had not gone very far when the ducks arrived.

They came paddling out from the reeds near the shore, in a loose, wobbly line, and fell in behind the ferry as if they had been waiting for it. There were eight of them. Arthur slowed the engine a little, so they could keep up.

The man in the tidy coat looked at the ducks, and then at Arthur. Do they always do that, he asked.

Every evening, said Arthur. They like the last crossing. I think it is their walk before bed.

The boy with the fishing rod, who had clearly heard all of this before, leaned over the side and said, tell him their names.

Arthur smiled. He pointed with his chin, because his hands were on the tiller. The one at the front, he said, is Admiral. She is in charge, and she knows it. The two behind her are Pickle and Biscuit. They are brothers, and they argue about everything. The one with the white patch on her head is Mrs. Henderson. She is very dignified. That little one paddling much too fast is Tuesday. I found him on a Tuesday. The two at the back are Rose and Rosie, and I am never quite sure which is which, and I do not think they are either.

That is seven, said the man in the tidy coat, who had been counting.

And there, said Arthur, nodding toward the reeds, is the eighth.

A last duck was paddling out from the shore, a little late, a little scruffy, with one feather sticking up on the top of his head like a question mark. He hurried to catch up with the others, and fell in at the very back of the line, slightly to one side.

That one, said Arthur, is Walter. Walter is always late. Walter has never once been on time for anything. But he always comes.

The woman with the basket of eggs laughed softly. The boy grinned. And the man in the tidy coat, for the first time, let go of the rail.

The ferry went putt, putt, putt across the middle of the lake. Out here the water was very deep and very calm, and the air was cool and smelled of reeds and wet stone. The sun had slipped behind the hills now, and the peach colors were fading into lavender, and then into a soft, deep blue. On the far shore, the first lights came on in the farmhouses, one, then another, then another, small and yellow and steady.

A fish jumped somewhere off to the left, and the rings it left behind spread out slowly across the water. The boy looked at them with deep personal disappointment. Arthur told him that the fish had been very impressed with his efforts today and would surely be easier to catch next time. The boy did not believe this, but he liked hearing it.

The ducks paddled on behind them. Pickle and Biscuit had a small disagreement, with a lot of quacking and some splashing, and then forgot about it. Mrs. Henderson ignored them both. Tuesday kept zooming ahead and then dropping back. Walter, at the back, kept paddling, steady and a little crooked.

The man in the tidy coat sat down on the bench. He watched the ducks for a long time. Then he said, quietly, I have had a very long week. And Arthur said, I know. Everyone who takes the last ferry has had a long week. That is what it is for.

Halfway across, Arthur did something he did every evening. He turned off the engine.

The silence that came after was enormous and gentle. There was no putt, putt, putt. There was only the soft lapping of water against the wooden sides, and the faint sound of the ducks paddling, and, from very far away, a dog barking once on one of the farms and then deciding that was enough. The ferry drifted. The sky was full of early stars now, and the lake was full of them too, so that the boat seemed to be floating in the middle of a great dark bowl of stars.

Nobody spoke. The woman with the eggs closed her eyes. The boy lay back on the bench with his hands behind his head. The man in the tidy coat loosened his tie, just a little, and breathed out for what seemed like a very long time.

After a minute, or maybe five, Arthur started the engine again. Putt, putt, putt. They moved on toward the far shore.

At the little wooden dock on the other side, the passengers got off one at a time. The woman with the eggs said good night and walked up the path to the farms. The boy ran off toward his grandmother's house, his rod bouncing on his shoulder, and his grandmother's porch light came on before he even got there. The man in the tidy coat stood on the dock for a moment and looked back at the lake, and then at Arthur.

Thank you, he said. I will take the last ferry again.

Arthur nodded. The ducks will be here, he said.

He tied up the boat for the night. The ducks drifted in around the dock, one by one, and tucked their heads under their wings among the reeds. Admiral first. Then Pickle and Biscuit, side by side, too tired to argue. Then Mrs. Henderson, with great dignity. Then Tuesday, finally still. Then Rose and Rosie, or Rosie and Rose.

And last of all, a little late, Walter, who paddled in slowly, found his place at the edge of the reeds, and settled down with a small, contented ruffle of feathers.

Arthur said good night to each of them by name. Then he turned off the lamp at the end of the dock, and the lake lay still and dark under the stars, and the only sound was the soft lap, lap, lap of the water against the wood.

stories.title: The Tortoise and the Strawberry
stories.text:
In the corner of an old walled garden, under a fig tree with leaves as big as dinner plates, there lived a tortoise named Agnes.

Agnes was very old. Nobody knew exactly how old. The family who owned the house had owned it for three generations, and Agnes had been in the garden for all of them. The grandmother remembered Agnes from when she was a little girl. The grandmother's grandmother had apparently remembered Agnes too. Agnes herself had never said, and nobody had ever thought it polite to ask.

The garden was a warm, sheltered place. The walls were made of old red brick, softened by moss and covered in climbing roses, and they held the heat of the sun long after the sun itself had gone. There were gravel paths and lavender bushes and a little round pond with a stone frog sitting on its edge. There were herb beds and a bench with peeling green paint. And in the far corner, the very farthest from the fig tree, there was the strawberry patch.

On this particular summer afternoon, Agnes woke up from her midday nap, put her head out of her shell, blinked twice, and decided that she would like a strawberry.

This was a big decision. The strawberry patch was all the way across the garden. For a person, it was perhaps forty steps. For Agnes, it was a journey.

She did not mind. Agnes had never been in a hurry in her life. She believed, in her slow and quiet way, that most of the good things in the world were still there when you arrived, as long as you kept going.

So she set off.

First she crossed the soft, cool grass under the fig tree. Each step was careful and deliberate. Front foot, other front foot, back foot, other back foot. Her shell rocked gently from side to side, like a little boat. The grass tickled the edges of her shell. A fig leaf drifted down and landed beside her, and she stopped to look at it for a while, because it was a very nice leaf, broad and green, with the sunlight shining through it. Then she walked on.

She reached the edge of the gravel path. The gravel was warm from the sun, and it crunched softly under her feet. Crunch, crunch, pause. Crunch, crunch, pause. A blackbird was hopping along the path ahead of her, looking for worms, and it stopped and looked back at her with one bright eye. Agnes looked back at the blackbird. The blackbird, apparently deciding that Agnes was not interesting enough to worry about, went back to its worms.

By the time Agnes reached the lavender, the shadows had moved a little across the garden. She walked slowly between the lavender bushes, and the scent was everywhere, sweet and sleepy. Bees were working in the purple flowers above her, humming softly, going from one flower to the next in no particular order. Agnes stopped under the lavender for a long rest. It was very pleasant there. The shade was cool and the hum of the bees was soothing. She closed her eyes for a while.

When she opened them again, the light had turned a little more golden.

She went on.

At the pond, she stopped for a drink. The water was cool and still, and her reflection looked back at her, an old, wise, slightly wrinkled face, with a shell like a small domed roof. The stone frog sat on the edge of the pond, as it always did, and Agnes looked at it, as she always did, and it said nothing, as it always did. Agnes thought it was probably the most patient creature in the garden, apart from herself.

A dragonfly hovered over the water, blue and shimmering. A little breeze moved the roses on the wall, and a few petals came drifting down, pink and white, and floated on the surface of the pond like tiny boats.

Agnes walked on, around the edge of the pond, past the herb beds. The thyme and the mint and the rosemary smelled warm and green. A small white butterfly landed on the top of her shell and rode along with her for a while, opening and closing its wings, before it flew off toward the roses. Agnes did not mind. She was happy to give it a lift.

The afternoon was getting older now. The sun was lower, and the light came slanting through the garden, long and golden, making the gravel paths glow and stretching the shadows of the bench and the fig tree all the way across the lawn. The air was softer. The birds were starting their evening songs, little trills and whistles from the tops of the walls.

In the house, someone opened a window, and the sound of a radio playing quiet music drifted out across the garden, along with the smell of supper cooking. Agnes lifted her head and listened for a moment. She liked the music. She did not know what it was, but it had been playing out of that window, on summer evenings, for a very long time.

At last, as the sun touched the top of the garden wall, Agnes arrived at the strawberry patch.

It was everything she had hoped. The leaves were thick and green, and underneath them, hanging low, were the strawberries. Some were still white and some were pink, but some were perfectly ripe, deep red, glowing in the evening light, smelling warm and sweet.

Agnes chose one. She took her time choosing, because it was an important decision, and in the end she chose one that was hanging very low, almost touching the ground, as if it had been waiting for her specifically. She took a small, slow bite. It was wonderful. It tasted of the whole summer afternoon, of sunshine and warm brick and slow walking.

She ate the strawberry very slowly, the way she did everything. When she had finished, she sat in the shade of the strawberry leaves and looked back across the garden at the long way she had come. The lawn. The fig tree. The lavender, the pond, the herb beds. The light was turning from gold to rose, and the walls glowed softly, giving back the warmth of the day.

The back door of the house opened, and the youngest child of the family came out in her pajamas, looking for Agnes, as she did every evening. She looked under the fig tree. She looked by the pond. And then she found her, in the strawberry patch, with a tiny bit of red juice on the end of her nose.

There you are, said the child softly. You walked all the way over here.

She did not pick Agnes up. The family had always known that Agnes preferred to walk. Instead, she sat down on the grass beside her, and the two of them watched the first star come out over the garden wall.

After a while, the child's mother called from the door, and the child said good night, and went back inside. The window closed. The music stopped. The garden grew quiet and blue.

Agnes tucked her head and her legs slowly into her shell. The strawberry leaves made a little green roof above her. The brick wall beside her was still warm, like a hand resting on her back. She would walk home tomorrow, she decided, or perhaps the day after. There was no hurry. There had never been any hurry.

And under the leaves, in the corner of the old walled garden, with the taste of summer still on her tongue, Agnes fell gently asleep.

stories.title: The Houseboat in the Rain
stories.text:
The canal ran quietly through the edge of the city, past old brick warehouses that had been turned into flats, under low stone bridges, and alongside a towpath lined with willow trees. Along one stretch, where the willows grew thickest, a line of narrow houseboats was moored, each one painted in a different color, each one with a little chimney on its roof.

The third boat along was dark green with cream trim, and its name was painted on the side in curling gold letters. It was called the Slow Hour. Nora lived there, with a kettle, a small iron stove, a great many books, and a large ginger cat named Marmalade.

It had been raining since the middle of the afternoon. Not a storm, just a soft, steady, settled rain, the kind of rain that sounds as if it has made itself comfortable and intends to stay all night. On a houseboat, you hear the rain more than anywhere else. It pattered on the roof, and drummed gently on the little hatch above the door, and dripped from the edges of the roof into the canal with a sound like someone tapping their fingers on a table, very slowly. Pat, pat, pat. Plip. Pat, pat.

Nora loved the rain on the boat. She always said it was like living inside a drum that was being played by someone very kind.

She had lit the stove an hour ago, and now the inside of the boat was warm and golden. The stove was small and black, with a little window in its door, and through the window you could see the orange flames moving. The boat smelled of wood smoke and old paper and the oranges that Nora kept in a bowl on the shelf.

The inside of the boat was long and narrow, like a hallway that someone had made into a home. At one end there was a tiny kitchen, with a two ring hob and a sink just big enough for one pot. In the middle there was a sitting area, with a low sofa covered in cushions and a little table that folded down from the wall. At the far end there was a bed, tucked under the curve of the roof, with a patchwork quilt and a round window that looked out at the water.

Marmalade was asleep on the sofa. He was a large cat, and he took up most of it. He was lying on his back with his paws in the air, which Nora thought was a very trusting way to sleep, and every now and then one of his ears twitched at the sound of the rain.

Nora filled the kettle and put it on the hob. While she waited for it to boil, she looked out of the little window by the kitchen. The canal was grey and dimpled with raindrops, thousands of tiny rings spreading and overlapping and fading. A pair of swans were gliding past, very slowly, close to the far bank, with their necks curved and their feathers beaded with water. On the towpath, a man walked by under a big black umbrella, with a small dog in a raincoat trotting beside him. The dog looked up at the boat, and Nora waved, and the dog wagged its tail, and they walked on into the grey.

Further along the towpath, the lamps were coming on, one by one. Each one made a soft yellow circle in the rain, and each circle had its own reflection, wobbling gently on the water of the canal.

The kettle began to sing, low at first, then higher. Nora took it off the hob just before it whistled, so as not to wake Marmalade. She made a pot of tea, strong and dark, and put a little milk in her favorite mug, the one with a chip on the handle, and carried it over to the sofa. She moved Marmalade's back legs gently to one side to make room. Marmalade did not wake up. He stretched, and sighed, and settled again, now with his head on her knee.

Nora had a book. It was an old book about a sailing voyage, with a faded blue cover and a smell of dust and salt. She had read it many times before. She liked books she had read before on rainy nights. You did not have to worry about what would happen. You could just let the words go by, like the water.

She read a few pages. She drank her tea. The rain went on. Pat, pat, pat. Plip.

Somewhere along the line of boats, someone was playing a guitar, very quietly, just a few chords over and over. The sound came drifting through the rain, soft and blurry, and then stopped. A little later, a door on another boat opened and closed, and someone laughed, and the laugh was warm and short and then it was quiet again.

The boat moved a little, now and then. Not much. Just a gentle rocking, as the wind pushed at the water, or as a duck paddled by close to the hull. Nora had lived on the boat for seven years, and she no longer noticed the rocking during the day. But at night, when everything else was still, she felt it, very softly, like being held.

After a while she put the book face down on her lap. She was not reading anymore. She was just listening. The rain on the roof. The crackle of the stove. The slow breathing of the cat. The soft creak of the mooring ropes as the boat shifted, just slightly, and settled again.

There is a particular feeling that comes on rainy nights, when you are warm and dry inside and the weather is going on outside without you. It is the feeling of being exactly where you are supposed to be. Nora had it now. It spread through her slowly, like the warmth from the tea.

She got up, carefully, so as not to disturb Marmalade, and put another log in the stove. She closed the little door, and the flames settled down to a gentle orange glow. She rinsed her mug in the tiny sink and put it upside down to dry. She looked out at the canal once more. The swans had gone. The towpath was empty. The lamps glowed in the rain.

Then she turned off the lamp by the sofa, so that the only light in the boat came from the little window of the stove. It painted the ceiling with soft, flickering orange shapes.

She walked down the narrow boat to the bed at the far end, and climbed in under the patchwork quilt. Through the round window by her pillow, she could see the dark water, and the raindrops making their rings, over and over, endlessly, and the yellow wobble of the nearest lamp.

A moment later there was a soft thump, and a weight at the bottom of the bed. Marmalade had woken up, noticed she had gone, and come to find her. He walked up the length of the quilt, turned around twice, and lay down against her side with a deep, rumbling purr.

The purr and the rain went together. Pat, pat, pat. Purr. Plip. Pat, pat.

Nora closed her eyes. The boat rocked, very gently. The stove ticked as it settled. The rain kept falling on the roof, on the canal, on the willows and the towpath and the sleeping city. And on the third boat along, the dark green one with the cream trim, the Slow Hour lived up to its name, and everyone inside it slept.

outro: And that is the end of tonight's stories. Let everything slow down now. The late bus is resting in the depot, the hives are humming under their blankets, and the puzzle is finished by the sleeping fire. The ducks are tucked in the reeds, the tortoise is asleep under the strawberry leaves, and the rain is still falling on the little green houseboat. There are more stories here on the channel, whenever you need them. But for now, just rest. Good night, and sleep well.
description:
Six cozy, original bedtime stories for grown-ups, read slowly to help you unwind and drift off.
A late night bus, a beekeeper tucking in her hives, a snowed in country inn, a ferry at dusk, a tortoise in a walled garden, and a houseboat in the rain.
No cliffhangers, no drama. Just soft rain, warm tea and quiet places.
Lights down, eyes closed. Good night from Snortlo 🌙
